notes: Interlocutory appeal on administrative transfer of a long TCC trial; full procedural reasoning available.

enrichment.short_title: Appeal against ex parte transfer of nine-week TCC trial from Liverpool to London
key_facts: Shawton Engineering claimed over £1.5 million against DGP for repudiatory breach and negligence in litigation marked by repeated claimant delay, aborted trial and indemnity costs orders.
After the claimants changed quantum experts and the June 2003 trial was vacated, the judge administratively transferred the case from Liverpool to the London TCC without hearing the parties.
The defendants objected that transfer would cost about £40,000 and disrupt a nine-week trial involving north-west witnesses, solicitors and parties.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against the judge's refusal to set aside his own-initiative administrative transfer order.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; transfer order discharged; case remitted to Salford with a new trial listing; costs of £9,000 agreed.
enrichment.ratio: A judge may not properly transfer a long trial to a distant venue on his own initiative without hearing the parties unless CPR 30.3(2) matters, especially convenience and expense, are so clear that no party input is needed; here the balance favoured trying the case in the North West.
legal_issues: Whether the judge acted improperly in transferring the case administratively without giving the parties a hearing
Whether convenience and expense to the parties should have outweighed keeping a London trial date
Whether an order made under CPR 3.3(4) must comply with CPR 3.3(5)(b) as to the right to apply to set aside

notes: Long public law appeal on Thames navigation rights and legitimate expectation; holdings taken from each judgment's conclusion.

enrichment.short_title: Whether Hedsor Water on the Thames remained private or subject to public navigation rights
key_facts: Mrs Rowland owned Hedsor Wharf on the Thames at Cookham, including banks and the river bed of Hedsor Water, a bypassed bend long treated by navigation authorities as private.
In late 2000 the Environment Agency concluded public rights of navigation still existed over Hedsor Water despite decades of weirs, signage and official plans marking it private.

The Agency's February 2001 letter accepted the Rowlands had bought on the assumption of privacy but said it would moderate the effect of reopening navigation rather than treat the water as permanently private.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from Lightman J's dismissal of Mrs Rowland's claim and his declarations that Hedsor Water remained subject to public rights of navigation.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed subject to a supplementary declaration that the Agency must take into account the pre-November 2000 common assumption of privacy as reflected in its February 2001 letter.
enrichment.ratio: Public rights of navigation over Hedsor Water were not permanently extinguished by long administrative treatment as private water; any legitimate expectation arising from the Agency's conduct was limited and satisfied by the assurances in its February 2001 letter rather than ongoing privacy or court supervision.
legal_issues: Whether Hedsor Water had become a permanently private water by statute or long practice
Whether Mrs Rowland had a legitimate expectation of privacy enforceable against the Environment Agency
Whether Article 8 and Article 1 Protocol 1 ECHR gave her possessory or privacy rights over the water
What declarations should govern future exercise of the Agency's statutory navigation functions

notes: Chancery appeal on strike-out and summary judgment in landlord consent dispute.

enrichment.short_title: Strike-out appeal on whether tenant's subletting consent request was properly formulated and served
key_facts: Norwich Union sought consent to underlet premises to E-Squared under a 1980 underlease and claimed damages for unreasonable delay after a 13 June 2002 solicitors' letter.
Mercantile Credit defended that the letter was not a valid consent request because it omitted proposed rent and was not validly served for purposes of the 1988 Act.
The parties had in fact treated the letter as an application for consent and progressed head-landlord consent before the landlord later relied on technical defences.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from Deputy Master Nurse's refusal to entertain, and dismissal of, an application to strike out parts of the defence or give summary judgment.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed in part: paragraph 6(a) of the defence struck out as having no real prospect of success; appeal dismissed on the service issue in paragraph 6(b), which must be resolved at trial.
enrichment.ratio: A court may refuse to determine a fragmentary interim application that would not shorten the trial and would add disproportionate cost, but a short implied-term point with no reasonable prospect of success may properly be decided early; service of a consent application under the 1988 Act was arguable and not suitable for summary judgment.
legal_issues: Whether a court may dismiss an application as contrary to the overriding objective without deciding its merits
Whether a request for underletting consent must specify proposed rent by an implied term in the lease
Whether service on the landlord's solicitors satisfied the 1988 Act and section 23 of the 1927 Act
Whether estoppel or conduct precluded the landlord from denying effective service

notes: Substantive family judgment on relocation, residence and contact in long-running private law dispute.

enrichment.short_title: Permission for father to relocate child to Shanghai and sole residence after harmful contact
key_facts: Eight-year-old Virad had lived with his father in Huddersfield since August 2001 after alleging his mother hit him; prior litigation had repeatedly found the mother's emotionally intense contact harmful.
Dr Cameron advised that staying contact profoundly disturbed Virad for weeks and ultimately recommended no direct contact unless the mother changed her behaviour.
The father, a Holset/Cummins executive, sought leave to take Virad to Shanghai for about three years for a career relocation with employer-funded schooling and support.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Final hearing of multiple applications including relocation, sole residence, contact enforcement and setting aside earlier contact orders.
enrichment.outcome: Father granted leave to remove Virad to Shanghai for three years from summer 2004; sole residence order to father; mother's set-aside and telephone contact enforcement applications dismissed; limited supervised contact ordered before relocation and potentially twice yearly thereafter.
enrichment.ratio: Applying Payne v Payne, a genuine and well-researched temporary relocation for career reasons may be permitted where the child's welfare requires remaining with the resident father and contact is already minimal; a shared residence order was inappropriate where the non-resident mother would have only supervised contact.
legal_issues: Whether leave to remove the child from the jurisdiction should be granted under Payne v Payne
Whether a sole residence order should replace the existing shared residence order
What contact, if any, was in the child's best interests given emotional harm from the mother
Whether security over the father's home and pension was required for return

notes: Appeal on standing and beneficial ownership in derivative action over misappropriated company funds used to buy property.

enrichment.short_title: Derivative action standing where misappropriated NLM funds traced into property held by director's wife
key_facts: Bracken Partners brought a derivative action for Eye Group Ltd against Ms Smalley and her husband over 52 Chatsworth Gardens, bought with £272,000 misappropriated from Non-League Media plc via EGL and GMG.
The deputy judge granted summary judgment declaring EGL beneficially entitled to 39/40 of the equity and ordering sale; net proceeds of about £212,000 were paid into court.
On appeal all parties accepted NLM was ultimately entitled to 39/40 of the proceeds and Ms Smalley to 1/40; the dispute centred on EGL's standing and costs.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against summary judgment and proprietary declaration in a derivative shareholder action.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; declaration amended to record that the 39/40 beneficial interest was held on trust for NLM.
enrichment.ratio: EGL had sufficient standing to bring proceedings to establish that Ms Smalley held the property on trust because it was personally accountable in equity for dishonest participation in misapplication of NLM's funds passing through its account, even though NLM remained the ultimate beneficial owner.
legal_issues: Whether EGL had title to sue for a proprietary interest after receiving and paying away misappropriated funds
Whether only NLM as beneficial owner could bring the proprietary claim
How the declaration should reflect agreed beneficial ownership of sale proceeds
Whether tracing and relative title principles defeated EGL's standing

notes: Appeal against summary disposal of sub-postmaster contract claims.

enrichment.short_title: Sub-postmaster's challenge to summary judgment on suspension pay and business losses
key_facts: Mr Lalji was suspended in July 1997 and summarily terminated in October 1997 after accounting irregularities and holding pension books against customer debts at his Poole Road post office and newsagent business.
He claimed withheld suspension remuneration, three months' pay in lieu of notice, losses to his ancillary business, and damages for harsh dismissal and psychiatric injury.
The Post Office relied on contract clauses allowing suspension without pay and forfeiture of withheld remuneration after termination.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against HHJ Mackay's order striking out parts of the claim and entering summary judgment for the Post Office.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed in part: claims for ancillary business loss and forfeited suspension remuneration may proceed to trial; claim for damages for manner of dismissal and psychiatric injury remains struck out.
enrichment.ratio: Forfeiture of remuneration under the sub-postmaster contract raised a triable issue under UCTA 1977 s 3(2)(b); associated business loss involved disputed causation and foreseeability unsuitable for summary judgment, but the manner-of-dismissal psychiatric claim faced insuperable factual and legal obstacles.
legal_issues: Whether clause 19(6) permitting forfeiture of withheld suspension pay was subject to the reasonableness test in UCTA 1977
Whether loss to the claimant's ancillary business from closure of the post office could succeed at trial
Whether summary judgment was appropriate for damages for humiliating dismissal and psychiatric injury
Whether the contract was a contract of employment for implied duty purposes

notes: Judicial review on leaving-care status under Children Act as amended.

enrichment.short_title: Whether care-leaver approaching 18 was a relevant and future former relevant child
key_facts: W, turning 18 on Christmas Day 2003, challenged Essex County Council's refusal to treat him as within the leaving-care regime.
He had been placed with foster carers under section 20 from February to September 2000 and given accommodation at the Park Hotel in July-August 2002 when aged 16.

The council had agreed to decide whether W was accommodated under section 20 and to reassess his needs; the parties ultimately accepted he was a relevant child and would become a former relevant child.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review with parallel wardship proceedings; wardship discharged and JR treated as lead proceedings.
enrichment.outcome: Declaration that W was a relevant child and would on turning 18 become a former relevant child; council to prepare pathway plan and appoint personal adviser; remaining grounds treated as academic.
enrichment.ratio: A child provided with accommodation while aged 16 could be 'looked after' for leaving-care purposes even if the authority characterised the placement under section 17; on the agreed facts W met the eligible and relevant child definitions and would acquire former relevant child status at 18.
legal_issues: Whether accommodation in 2002 made W a child looked after by the local authority
Whether W satisfied the eligible and relevant child definitions in the leaving-care code
Whether post-2002 amendments excluding section 17 accommodation from section 22 applied retrospectively
Whether past assessment failures remained live after the council's revised decision

notes: Complex fire-loss appeal on architect duty and contributory negligence apportionment.

enrichment.short_title: Architect liability for fire spread from gas bratt pan and contributory negligence apportionment
key_facts: A January 1998 fire started in a gas bratt pan at Sahib Foods' Southall factory and destroyed most of the building; total loss was about £27 million.
PKS architects had specified combustible EPS panels in the veg prep area despite warnings from insulation specialists about cooking and frying risks.

Fire experts agreed that fire-resistant compartmentation would have contained the blaze in room G49; Sahib was seriously at fault in causing the fire but had conceded 50% contributory negligence at trial.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against liability findings and refusal to apportion damages for contributory negligence after a split liability trial.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal on liability dismissed; appeal on contributory negligence allowed; damages recoverable from PKS reduced by two-thirds so Sahib may recover one-third of spread-of-fire loss.
enrichment.ratio: Architects who failed to investigate frying operations using deep oil and to specify fire-resistant panels were liable for spread of a foreseeable tenant-caused fire; the claimant was also contributorily negligent both in starting the fire and through its production manager's misleading statements to the insulation specialist, warranting a two-thirds reduction.
legal_issues: Whether PKS breached their duty by not advising fire-resistant panels in room G49
What depth of oil was used in cooking and whether PKS should have ascertained it
Whether Sahib's fault in causing the fire counted as contributory negligence to spread damage
Whether Mr Reynolds misleading LRI about steam-only cooking was contributory negligence

notes: Clinical negligence trial on chicken pox counselling in pregnancy; breach found but causation failed.

enrichment.short_title: Failure to ensure pregnant woman understood severity of fetal chicken pox risk — causation not proved
key_facts: Mrs Deriche contracted chicken pox at about 14-17 weeks' gestation in May 1996 and was counselled at Ealing Hospital that there was a small risk of transplacental spread and congenital malformation.

At a 5 June antenatal appointment she insisted on seeing consultant Mr Haeri, who reassured her the risk was low and termination was not needed but did not ensure she understood the nature and severity of possible abnormalities.

Her son Gabriel was born severely disabled in November 1996; experts agreed the risk was about 2% and that a consultant should have illustrated major possible abnormalities rather than rely on A&E notes.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court liability trial in obstetric negligence; causation tried at same hearing.
enrichment.outcome: Breach of duty established against Mr Haeri but claim failed because Mrs Deriche did not prove she would have terminated had proper counselling been given.
enrichment.ratio: A consultant who sees an upset patient specifically about termination must satisfy himself she understands the severity of fetal risks, not merely assume earlier A&E counselling sufficed; but where the patient had already accepted a small risk after full registrar counselling and wished to continue the pregnancy, better consultant counselling would likely have produced the same decision.
legal_issues: Whether Mr Haeri's 5 June consultation met the Bolam standard for informed advice
Whether he was entitled to rely on Dr Adedze's A&E note of full counselling without revisiting severity of abnormalities
Whether Mrs Deriche would have opted for termination if properly advised
How Wyatt v Curtis affects duties of a second doctor seeing the patient later
